title: Putting Students Ahead of Politics
author: Beanie Geoghegan
summary: Writing the morning after the midterm elections, Beanie Geoghegan says her concern is not partisan politics but the future of K-12 education after a few years of bipartisan reform. She traces the progress since 2020: parents of every political leaning who homeschooled, ran for school boards, backed school choice or started micro schools, and leaders who refocused schools on academics. She credits specific wins, including the move away from three-cueing toward research-informed reading instruction, Louisiana's Let Teachers Teach discipline policy that other states copied, and a growing agreement around E.D. Hirsch's case for knowledge-rich curriculum. She also names expanded school choice through vouchers, education savings accounts and tax credits as a change that let more families take ownership. Her worry is that incoming leaders, such as a governor-elect who promised to fire Texas Education Commissioner Mike Morath, may abandon reforms for political reasons. She concludes that adults have spent too much time on their own preferences and that students cannot afford to start over each time leadership changes.
points: Geoghegan frames the reform wave since 2020 as bipartisan, driven by parents of all political leanings who took more direct ownership of their children's schooling.
She lists three practical gains: research-based reading instruction replacing three-cueing, teacher authority over classroom discipline, and a push for content-rich curriculum.
Louisiana's Let Teachers Teach policy, which lets teachers remove disruptive students, is held up as the model that West Virginia, Alabama and Texas followed.
School choice tools such as vouchers, education savings accounts and scholarship tax credits are presented as giving families without means real alternatives.
Her central worry is that reforms with strong results could be reversed purely for political reasons, forcing students to keep starting over.
quotes: Before you move past this out of weariness with politics, please know this isn't an essay about politics. This is about education and what the future of K-12 education looks like for tens of millions of children.
It was refreshing to see the focus of schools return to academics after too many years spent fixated on political and social justice issues and culture wars.

First up was eliminating ineffective reading instruction (e.g., three-cueing) from elementary classrooms and adopting research-informed practices. Teachers (mostly) cheered and embraced a clear, coherent method of teaching students how to read.
Teachers can’t teach, and students can’t learn in chaos. When violent and disruptive student behavior is ignored or excused by administrators, chaos ensues.
Knowledge matters a lot. What students come to school knowing has a tremendous impact on how easily or quickly they will learn.

It’s concerning that positive reforms for students would be abandoned simply because of political differences. That seems quite unfair to the children who will be negatively impacted. Students cannot afford to keep starting over every time political leadership changes.
When it comes to K-12 education in our country, adults have spent far too much time thinking about what they want or prefer and far too little time considering what is best for students.
